critic_changes: Checked all ten quoted passages against the text of IMF Country Reports 25/312 and 25/313. WebFetch could not decode the PDFs, so the critic extracted their text locally. Every passage appears near-verbatim, the dates (November 2025) match the documents, and both sources are tier 1 and recent. All citations kept.

Checked every number against desk/data/SMR.json. These all match as rounded: 2.7, -4.4 and 2.4 (eras); 14.1 (2009); 6.9 (2020); 15.6 (2021); 9.5 (2022); 0.1 (2023); 18.2 (shortfall); 1998 (level first reached). The claim that income fell every year from 2008 to 2012 also matches the series.

Pandemic thread: the draft called both 2021 and 2022 'the fastest growth in the series', but only 2021 (15.6) is the series high; 1999 (7.7) and 2022 (9.5) are lower. Reworded so the claim applies only to 2021.

Bank clean-up and public debt thread: the eurobond's 2027 due date was not in any cited passage, so a third citation from CR 25/312 that names the 2027 maturity was added. 'But remains high' was dropped because no cited passage supported it.

Workers thread: 'Jobs are at record highs' was not supported by the only citation, so a CR 25/312 passage on record employment was added. 'Commute daily from nearby Italian regions' was changed to 'foreign workers who commute in daily' to match the quoted passage.

Tension: the IMF's 'booming' description refers to 2024-25, while the data end in 2023. The text now dates the IMF's view to late 2025 and says the data end in 2023, so the two periods are not run together. 'Commuters from Italy' was changed to 'workers who commute in from abroad' to match the cited wording.

No banned phrases or recommendation or verdict language found. 5 threads and 2 distinct recent tier 1 sources survive, so the story stays tier 1. The process note that WebSearch was not run is kept in sources_searched.

growth_story.headline: San Marino's income per person fell hard after its oversized banks hit crisis in 2009; a shift to factories and tourism has won back only part of the loss.
growth_story.arc: Income per person in San Marino grew 2.7 percent a year from 1998 to 2007, when it reached its peak, at a time when the country carried a financial sector the IMF later called oversized. From 2008 to 2015 it shrank 4.4 percent a year: the global financial crisis hit that sector, a banking crisis began in 2009, and income per person fell 14.1 percent in 2009 alone. Since 2016 growth has averaged 2.4 percent a year, as the economy moved away from finance toward manufacturing, exports of nonfinancial services and tourism. That era included a fall of 6.9 percent in 2020 with the pandemic, then gains of 15.6 percent in 2021 and 9.5 percent in 2022. Even so, income per person in 2023 was still 18.2 percent below the 2007 peak and about where it first was in 1998.

growth_story.tension: The IMF's late-2025 review describes a booming economy, with record employment and strong wage growth. But in the data, which end in 2023, income per person grew just 0.1 percent that year and was still 18.2 percent below its 2007 peak, about where it first was in 1998. Part of the gap may lie in what is counted: many jobs are held by workers who commute in from abroad, which is why the IMF prefers output per worker to output per resident as a gauge.
